About context for the new chat

You do not need to paste all the context. Memory auto-loads each session (the index + those four notes), so a short prompt is enough. Here's one that's self-contained and points at the memory:

Continue the GuideMate capstone. Step 1 (getting the TurtleBot4 Gazebo sim
working on my WSL2 laptop) is DONE — the fix was switching WSL from mirrored to
NAT networking. Full context is in my memory files (MEMORY.md + the guidemate-*
notes) — read those first.

Now let's build MVP #1: a name→Nav2 navigation system — I publish a destination
NAME (typed string via ROS topic/CLI) and the namespaced TB4 autonomously drives
there in sim, lidar-only. The plan, locked decisions, and fleet-shaped
architecture are in the guidemate-mvp-plan memory.

Start the sim with:  bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh   (I'll run it in a dedicated
terminal so it persists). Then let's begin step 2 of the build order (the map).
Work with me interactively, and step back to high-level differences before
drilling into details.

Where we are

Step 1 is genuinely closed: healthy DDS in NAT mode, robot drives, sensors work, LEDs confirmed-cosmetic. Next chat picks up at step 2 — the map (my recommendation there will be to SLAM the existing maze first to get end-to-end navigation working fast, then build a custom DIY world — but we'll decide together).

One tip for the new session: start the sim yourself with bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh in its own terminal before we begin — that avoids the background-launch-dies-at-session-boundary problem we hit today, so the sim stays up while we work.

Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

12	**MVP #1 definition of done:** "In a headless DIY Gazebo world, publish a destination NAME (typed string via ROS topic/CLI) and one namespaced TB4 autonomously navigates there, faster-than-realtime, LIDAR-ONLY (no camera — privacy)."
13	
14	**Locked decisions (Shibo):**
15	- Sim-only first (Jazzy); real Humble TB4 is a later port (TurtleBot4Navigator API differs).
16	- Command interface = local ROS topic + CLI now. AWS IoT/MQTT deferred (AWS IoT is just a cloud MQTT broker — unneeded for a single-laptop sim; wire it later as a transport in front of the same nav core).
17	- LLM/voice DEFERRED — typed string first, so the LLM workstream doesn't block the demo.
18	- No camera/image topics (privacy); lidar only.
19	
20	**Why sim (Shibo's research angle):** stress-test coordination hardware can't — high-concurrency dispatch across many robots, and multi-robot cooperation/handoff (robot A escorts to floor-2 elevator, robot B takes over on floor 14). So MVP #1 is single-robot in behavior but **fleet-shaped in structure** from day one.
21	
22	**Architecture (3 layers):** (1) Robot layer = per-robot namespaced Nav2 stack (namespace is already a launch arg, e.g. robot_1); (2) Dispatcher layer = fleet node that decides which robot handles a request (trivial for 1 robot now; the research-rich part later); (3) Input adapter layer = thin front-ends (CLI/topic now; MQTT/voice/LLM later) all calling the same nav core. Data model: destination `{name, floor, x, y, θ}` (include `floor` now, used later); floor/elevator topology graph = stub now.
23	
24	**Build order:** (1) verify stack — DONE; (2) build DIY world (simple rooms/corridor) — or SLAM the existing `maze` first for speed; (3) generate nav map (slam_toolbox + map_saver → .pgm/.yaml); (4) capture named-destination poses (drive robot + read /robot_1/sim_ground_truth_pose; no RViz needed); (5) headless + faster-than-realtime (custom launch: `gz sim -s`, physics real_time_factor); (6) nav core node (name→pose lookup→Nav2 goal) + trivial dispatcher + CLI adapter; (7) end-to-end test. See [[guidemate-sim-facts]].

23	- Nav2 launchers: `turtlebot4_navigation` {nav2, localization, slam}.launch.py.

Launch: `bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh [world]` (default world=maze; also depot/warehouse). The script clears stale DDS env + `/dev/shm`, then runs `ros2 launch turtlebot4_gz_bringup turtlebot4_gz.launch.py namespace:=robot_1 rviz:=false world:=<world>`. **Run it in a dedicated terminal so the sim persists** (background launches via the agent die at session boundaries). Software rendering (LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1) → slow; diffdrive controller takes ~30s to activate.

Confirmed healthy in NAT mode: 0 SHM errors, `ros2` daemon works, scan + odom + cmd_vel all deliver, robot drives.

Key facts:
- Drive: publish `geometry_msgs/msg/Twist` to `/robot_1/cmd_vel_unstamped` (no timestamp check). (`/robot_1/cmd_vel` takes TwistStamped but needs a valid sim-time stamp; diffdrive use_stamped_vel=false, cmd_vel_timeout=0.5s drops stale msgs.)

- Robot spawns UNDOCKED (dock_status is_docked:false) — no undock needed. Undock action exists at `/robot_1/undock` (irobot_create_msgs/action/Undock) if ever docked.
- Dark HMI LEDs are COSMETIC ONLY: turtlebot4_node needs create3 hardware services (start_motor, etc.) absent in sim, and the HMI GUI plugin's namespace is empty. Zero functional impact — ignore them; verify health by watching the robot move instead.
- Gazebo runs as `ruby` processes (comm=ruby), NOT `gz` — `pgrep`/`ps` for gazebo must account for that.
- No headless flag in stock launch (GUI hardcoded in sim.launch.py; turtlebot4_gz.launch.py does not forward gz_args). A custom launch is needed later for headless (`gz sim -s`) and faster-than-realtime (physics real_time_factor).
- Nav2 launchers: `turtlebot4_navigation` {nav2, localization, slam}.launch.py.
See [[guidemate-mvp-plan]].

1	---
2	name: guidemate-wsl-networking-nat-switch
3	description: GuideMate laptop WSL networking — mirrored mode broke ROS2 DDS; switched to NAT (CONFIRMED FIXED)
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: project
7	  originSessionId: 284b9a61-fe1d-4aea-966d-750802f95c6d
8	---
9	
10	STATUS 2026-07-04: FIXED & CONFIRMED. Switching WSL from mirrored to NAT solved the sim; step 1 is done.
11	
12	Problem: On Shibo's Lenovo laptop (AMD 6900HS + RTX 3050), the ROS2 Jazzy + Gazebo TB4 sim launched but inter-node DDS comm was broken/degraded — dark LEDs, controllers slow (125s) or failing, `ros2 topic list` daemon hanging, flaky topic delivery, hundreds of SHM `open_and_lock_file` errors.
13	
14	Root cause: WSL2 **mirrored** networking mode (`/mnt/c/Users/76405/.wslconfig` had `networkingMode=mirrored`, `firewall=true`). Mirrored makes ROS nodes share the Windows network stack, so DDS crosses the Hyper-V firewall + a messy interface set (loopback0, extra lo addr 10.255.255.254, /16 eth2). Decisive proof it was the network (not SHM/scripts): comm failed even with shared memory fully disabled. Ruled out: hardware (GPU idle under software rendering) and SHM (harmless UDP-fallback noise, maybe worsened by Lenovo OEM security). The Canada desktop had worked because it used NAT.
15	
16	Fix applied: `.wslconfig` → `[wsl2] networkingMode=NAT / dnsTunneling=true / autoProxy=false` (original saved to `.wslconfig.mirrored.bak`). Proxy in `~/.bashrc` changed from Clash@127.0.0.1:7890 (mirrored) to Windows-host-IP: `WIN_HOST=$(ip route show default | awk '{print $3}')` → `http(s)_proxy=http://$WIN_HOST:7890`, `all_proxy=socks5://$WIN_HOST:7891` — **requires Clash "Allow LAN" enabled**. Takes effect via `wsl --shutdown` from Windows.
17	
18	Confirmed after restart: single clean eth0, proxy works (curl → HTTP 200), sim fully healthy (0 SHM errors, diffdrive controller up in ~30s, ros2 daemon OK, robot drives). See [[guidemate-sim-facts]], [[debugging-step-back-over-detail-drilling]].
19

3	description: How Shibo wants debugging approached — step back to environment/architecture differences before drilling into detail-level fixes
4	metadata:

9	
10	When debugging fails, Shibo strongly prefers stepping back to consider high-level differences (environment, architecture, machine-to-machine differences) BEFORE drilling into detail-level config patches.
11	
12	**Why:** "Mono-directional drilling" — change one small variable, relaunch the whole stack (~60s), repeat — wasted ~an hour chasing symptoms (proxy, discovery server, shared memory, UDP-only transport) when the real root cause was a high-level environment difference (WSL mirrored vs NAT networking). A key clue was walked past twice, and a self-inflicted test-script bug (a QoS mismatch) was masked by the churn.
13	
14	**How to apply:** When something doesn't work, first ask "what's fundamentally different here vs a known-good setup?" Isolate variables with cheap standalone tests instead of nuking/relaunching the full stack. Verify the obvious early (QoS compatibility, warning logs). Be decisive — give a reasoned recommendation, not a string of trial-and-error attempts. See [[guidemate-wsl-networking-nat-switch]].

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# GuideMate TB4 Gazebo sim launcher (WSL2 ROS2 Jazzy, NAT networking).
# Run in a DEDICATED terminal so the sim persists:  bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh [world]
# worlds: maze (default) | depot | warehouse
set -u
WORLD="${1:-maze}"

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
# clear any stale DDS overrides left from past debugging (NAT default is correct)
unset ROS_DISCOVERY_SERVER ROS_SUPER_CLIENT FASTRTPS_DEFAULT_PROFILES_FILE \
      ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE FASTDDS_BUILTIN_TRANSPORTS
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0
export LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1

# kill any previous sim and wipe stale shared-memory locks (WSL FastDDS quirk)
pkill -9 -f "turtlebot4_gz_bringup" 2>/dev/null
pkill -9 -f "ros_gz_bridge"          2>/dev/null
pkill -9 -f "gz sim"                 2>/dev/null
sleep 2
rm -f /dev/shm/fastrtps_* /dev/shm/sem.fastrtps_* /dev/shm/*fastdds* 2>/dev/null

echo "[sim_start] launching TB4 (world=$WORLD, namespace=robot_1) ..."
exec ros2 launch turtlebot4_gz_bringup turtlebot4_gz.launch.py \
  namespace:=robot_1 rviz:=false world:="$WORLD"

Here's where we are: ROS 2 Jazzy env is live in my shell, `slam_toolbox` is installed, but **the sim isn't running** (no gazebo/ruby procs, no ROS nodes) and there are **no maps yet** in `~/robotics`. So step 2 is a clean start.

## Stepping back — what "step 2: the map" actually is

Before touching config, the high-level fork. A Nav2 map is just a `.pgm` + `.yaml` file on disk — it's completely decoupled from *which world* produced it and from *all* the nav code we write later. That means the world-building question and the get-nav-working question are separable, and we can order them for lowest risk:

**Two ways to get that map file:**

| | SLAM the existing `maze` world | Build a DIY world first, then SLAM it |
|---|---|---|
| Time to a usable map | ~minutes (drive + save) | hours (SDF authoring) + then SLAM |
| Validates the real pipeline | Yes — SLAM→save→AMCL→Nav2 end-to-end on a known-good world | Same, but gated behind world-building |
| Throwaway risk | Map is disposable; nav code is not | World-building effort sunk before nav proven |

My recommendation (matches the plan): **SLAM the existing `maze` first.** It gets end-to-end navigation working fast and de-risks the hard integration (nav core + dispatcher). The DIY world is a separate SDF-authoring skill we can swap in later — it changes the `.pgm/.yaml`, not a line of nav code.

content.text:
Good question — and the answer flips depending on one environmental fact about your laptop, so let me step back to that first.

## The two knobs do different things

- **Sim clock (`real_time_factor`)** = a *multiplier* on how fast sim-time advances vs wall-clock. Crucial catch: it's **capped by spare compute**. If your machine can't even keep up with real-time, asking for 2× does nothing — Gazebo just runs as fast as it can and ignores the target.
- **Robot speed** = reduces the *amount of simulation* needed to cover the maze (fewer sim-seconds of driving), completely independent of RTF.

## The decisive fact for *your* laptop

You're running `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` → **llvmpipe CPU software rendering** (the RTX 3050 isn't in the loop under WSL). The Gazebo GUI's render loop is the dominant CPU cost, and it almost certainly pins you **at or below RTF 1.0 already**.

That means: **the clock knob is effectively dead on your machine right now.** You have no spare compute for it to use. So between your two options —

**→ Tune the robot's speed, not the clock.** It's the only one of the two that helps given your compute ceiling.

**But with guardrails** — the goal is a *good map*, not a fast lap. Fast rotation is what wrecks SLAM (scan smear → failed loop closure). So:
- Linear: push near TB4's max (~0.30 m/s) — safe, this is your main time-saver.
- Angular: keep gentle (~0.5–0.8 rad/s) — turns are where map quality dies.

## The lever you *didn't* ask about — and it's the bigger one

The real unlock is **going headless** (`gz sim -s`, no GUI render). That removes the rendering bottleneck, which is what *makes the clock knob work again* — freed CPU → RTF can climb → then faster-than-realtime is real. That's exactly step 5 in the plan. The nuance: it's a custom-launch project (stock launch has no headless flag), and it pays off for *all* nav testing later, not just this one SLAM drive.

## Revised step 2 plan

1. **Verify the premise first (cheap, ~30s).** Start the sim, read actual RTF (`gz stats` / world stats topic). This confirms whether you're compute-bound before we commit. Matches your "verify the obvious early" rule — I don't want to assume RTF < 1 if your machine surprises us.
2. **For this one SLAM drive: don't build headless yet.** Bump robot linear speed, keep turns gentle, drive the maze once. SLAM is inherently a short drive; not worth a launch-file project to shave it.
3. **Watch the map build in RViz, not Gazebo GUI.** RViz rendering an occupancy grid + laser scan is far cheaper than Gazebo's full 3D physics render — you get feedback without the heavy render cost.
4. **Move the headless + RTF-boost custom launch to its proper home (step 5)**, where it accelerates the repeated nav test-loops that actually dominate your wall-clock later.

Net: **speed knob now (with quality guardrails), clock knob later once headless earns it.**

To confirm point 1, start the sim in your dedicated terminal:

```
bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh
```

Once it's up, tell me and I'll read the real RTF — if by some chance you've got headroom, I'll revise and we'll use the clock too. Sound good?

content.text:
Now the bottleneck is clear. The maze physics is stock (1ms step, 1000 Hz), but look at the sensor list — this robot+dock renders a *pile* of sensors, and on WSL's latency-bound d3d12 path **each rendered sensor is a serialized GPU round-trip**:

- **4 dock sensors** (green/red/yellow buoy + halo) — the standard dock, which we don't need at all
- **4 cliff sensors** (rendered scans)
- **OAK-D RGBD camera** — unused, and against your lidar-only privacy rule
- the **main 2D lidar** — the only one SLAM actually needs

Low GPU + low CPU + capped RTF = we're paying latency for ~10 rendered sensors when we need 1. That's the lever, not the clock or robot speed. Let me check whether the launch lets us drop the dock and GUI cheaply (config args beat model surgery):

import os

from pathlib import Path

from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory

from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument
from launch.actions import IncludeLaunchDescription, SetEnvironmentVariable
from launch.launch_description_sources import PythonLaunchDescriptionSource
from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration, PathJoinSubstitution
from launch_ros.actions import Node


ARGUMENTS = [
    DeclareLaunchArgument('use_sim_time', default_value='true',
                          choices=['true', 'false'],
                          description='use_sim_time'),
    DeclareLaunchArgument('world', default_value='warehouse',
                          description='Simulation World'),
    DeclareLaunchArgument('model', default_value='lite',
                          choices=['standard', 'lite'],
                          description='Turtlebot4 Model'),
]


def generate_launch_description():

    # Directories
    pkg_turtlebot4_gz_bringup = get_package_share_directory(
        'turtlebot4_gz_bringup')
    pkg_turtlebot4_gz_gui_plugins = get_package_share_directory(
        'turtlebot4_gz_gui_plugins')
    pkg_turtlebot4_description = get_package_share_directory(
        'turtlebot4_description')
    pkg_irobot_create_description = get_package_share_directory(
        'irobot_create_description')
    pkg_irobot_create_gz_bringup = get_package_share_directory(
        'irobot_create_gz_bringup')
    pkg_irobot_create_gz_plugins = get_package_share_directory(
        'irobot_create_gz_plugins')
    pkg_ros_gz_sim = get_package_share_directory(
        'ros_gz_sim')

    # Set Gazebo resource path
    gz_resource_path = SetEnvironmentVariable(
        name='GZ_SIM_RESOURCE_PATH',
        value=':'.join([
            os.path.join(pkg_turtlebot4_gz_bringup, 'worlds'),
            os.path.join(pkg_irobot_create_gz_bringup, 'worlds'),
            str(Path(pkg_turtlebot4_description).parent.resolve()),
            str(Path(pkg_irobot_create_description).parent.resolve())
        ])
    )

    gz_gui_plugin_path = SetEnvironmentVariable(
        name='GZ_GUI_PLUGIN_PATH',
        value=':'.join([
            os.path.join(pkg_turtlebot4_gz_gui_plugins, 'lib'),
            os.path.join(pkg_irobot_create_gz_plugins, 'lib')
        ])
    )

    # Paths
    gz_sim_launch = PathJoinSubstitution(
        [pkg_ros_gz_sim, 'launch', 'gz_sim.launch.py'])

    # Gazebo harmonic
    gazebo = IncludeLaunchDescription(
        PythonLaunchDescriptionSource([gz_sim_launch]),
        launch_arguments=[
            ('gz_args', [
                LaunchConfiguration('world'),
                '.sdf',
                ' -r',
                ' -v 4',
                ' --gui-config ',
                PathJoinSubstitution([
                    pkg_turtlebot4_gz_bringup,
                    'gui',
                    LaunchConfiguration('model'),
                    'gui.config'
                ])
            ])
        ]
    )

    # Clock bridge
    clock_bridge = Node(package='ros_gz_bridge', executable='parameter_bridge',
                        name='clock_bridge',
                        output='screen',
                        arguments=[
                            '/clock' + '@rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock' + '[gz.msgs.Clock'
                        ])

    # Create launch description and add actions
    ld = LaunchDescription(ARGUMENTS)
    ld.add_action(gz_resource_path)
    ld.add_action(gz_gui_plugin_path)
    ld.add_action(gazebo)
    ld.add_action(clock_bridge)
    return ld

    )

        package='ros_gz_bridge', executable='parameter_bridge', name='clock_bridge',

            ('x', LaunchConfiguration('x')),
            ('y', LaunchConfiguration('y')),
            ('z', LaunchConfiguration('z')),
            ('yaw', LaunchConfiguration('yaw'))]
    )

    ld = LaunchDescription(ARGUMENTS)
    ld.add_action(gz_resource_path)
    ld.add_action(gazebo)
    ld.add_action(clock_bridge)
    ld.add_action(robot_spawn)
    return ld

Removing the GUI removed a render pass that wasn't the constraint.

1. **Fewer render submits** → strip unused sensors (camera, dock, cliff) — certain to help, but model surgery.
2. **Lower per-submit latency** → this is the untested one, and there's a strong theory: the discrete RTX 3050 sits behind PCIe + WSL virtualization (high latency per submit), while the **AMD iGPU is on-die (low latency)**. description: GuideMate sim was 66x too slow (RTF 0.015) because it forced CPU software rendering; fix = GPU via WSLg d3d12
metadata:
  type: project
---

STATUS 2026-07-05: FIXED. During step 2 (SLAM), found the sim ran at RTF **0.015** (~66x slower than real-time) — SLAM/nav infeasible.

Root cause: `sim_start.sh` set `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1`, a leftover crutch from step-1 debugging (unrelated to the NAT networking fix). It forced Gazebo to render on llvmpipe (CPU), pinning RTF to 0.015 with 10/16 cores idle — i.e. NOT CPU-count-bound, it was the software-GL path.

Fix: use the GPU via WSLg. The RTX 3050 is reachable (`/dev/dxg`, `/usr/lib/wsl/lib/libd3d12*.so`, `nvidia-smi` works) and Mesa's `d3d12_dri.so` is installed. `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE` off alone still defaults to llvmpipe — must FORCE it: `export GALLIUM_DRIVER=d3d12` (+ `MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME=NVIDIA` for the discrete card, or `AMD` for the on-die iGPU). Verify with `glxinfo -B | grep renderer` → should say `D3D12 (NVIDIA/AMD ...)` not llvmpipe. `sim_start.sh` now sets these; needs `mesa-utils` for glxinfo (installed).

Result ladder (world=maze): software 0.015 → NVIDIA+GUI 0.067 → NVIDIA headless 0.052 → **AMD iGPU headless 0.069** (4.6x). Also fixed: `sim_start.sh` had `set -u` which crashed on ROS `setup.bash` (unbound AMENT_TRACE_SETUP_FILES) — now wrapped in `set +u`/`set -u`.

**Remaining ceiling ~0.07 is per-render-submit latency in the WSL d3d12 paravirtualization layer** — identical for both GPUs, unaffected by killing the GUI. ~10 rendered sensors (main lidar + 4 cliff + 4 dock buoy/halo + OAK-D camera) each submit a render per cycle; the round-trip latency × submit count is the cap (confirmed: GPU only ~11-38% util, gz server <1 core, yet RTF stuck). ONLY lever left = fewer sensors. Deferred to step 5: a lean/headless custom launch stripping camera+cliff+dock to lidar-only (potential RTF ~0.3-0.5), where repeated nav test-loops benefit. For the one-time SLAM drive we accepted ~0.07 + fast driving. New file: `~/robotics/sim_start_headless.sh` + `~/robotics/sim_headless.launch.py` (server-only `gz sim -s`, reuses stock spawn). Clock knob is useless below RTF 1.0; robot-SPEED is the only useful runtime lever once GPU fix is in. See [[guidemate-sim-facts]], [[guidemate-mvp-plan]].

Confirmed fully down, GPU idle. It crashed on its own — and notably, the **AMD iGPU headless** config is the one config that didn't survive (NVIDIA-GUI and NVIDIA-headless both ran stably during testing). That points at iGPU instability under WSL's d3d12 layer.

```
bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh
```

Rationale — for the SLAM drive specifically, this config wins on the axes that matter:
- **Stable** (ran fine during our GPU test), where AMD-headless just crashed.
- **NVIDIA** (the discrete card was stable; the iGPU wasn't).
- **~0.067 RTF** — same ballpark as headless anyway (the WSL render latency ceiling dominates regardless).
- **GUI gives visual feedback** — genuinely useful while watching a SLAM map build, on top of RViz.

The marginal headless speed edge isn't worth re-crashing a 20-minute drive. Paste the crash lines if you have them, then launch `sim_start.sh` and tell me when it's up — I'll bring up slam_toolbox and we'll start mapping.

content.text:
Ah — **I misdiagnosed that, my apologies.** Look at the top line: `^C [WARNING] [launch]: user interrupted with ctrl-c (SIGINT)`. The sim didn't crash — it received a **Ctrl-C** and shut down cleanly (every node reports "finished cleanly"; the `exit code -15` at the end is just Gazebo taking >5s to stop during normal shutdown). So my "AMD iGPU is unstable" theory was wrong — **retract that**; the iGPU headless config is fine, it was just interrupted.

That also means my earlier TF check ("no /tf topics") was unreliable — the sim was already down by then. The shutdown log actually *confirms* the TF publishers exist (`robot_state_publisher`, many `static_transform_publisher`, `pose_republisher_node`), so TF should be fine once it's freshly up.

Let me not over-think the relaunch config since AMD-headless and NVIDIA-GUI are the same speed (~0.07). For the SLAM drive I'll go with the **standard GUI launch** — simplest, and seeing the robot in Gazebo alongside RViz is handy while mapping:

```
bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh
```

Once it's up (~30s for the controller), tell me — I'll first re-verify the TF tree (`odom→base_link→laser`) properly this time, then bring up slam_toolbox and we start mapping.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""GuideMate SLAM driver: reactive left-hand wall-follower (lidar-only).

Drives the namespaced TB4 around a maze to build a slam_toolbox map, hands-off.
- Subscribes /robot_1/scan (SensorDataQoS = BEST_EFFORT, matches the gz lidar).
- Publishes geometry_msgs/Twist to /robot_1/cmd_vel_unstamped (no stamp check).
Left-hand rule: keep the wall on the LEFT at ~target distance; turn right when the
front is blocked; curve left to reacquire when the left opens up. Speeds kept modest
so SLAM scan-matching stays clean (fast rotation smears loop closure).
"""
import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist

NS = '/robot_1'

# tunables
TARGET_LEFT = 0.55     # desired distance to left wall (m)
FRONT_STOP = 0.65      # if anything closer than this ahead, turn away
LIN_SPEED = 0.22       # forward speed (m/s); TB4 max ~0.31
TURN = 0.9             # base angular speed (rad/s)
HYST = 0.12            # deadband around TARGET_LEFT (m)
SECTOR = math.radians(25)  # half-width of each sampling sector


class WallFollower(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('wall_follower')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, f'{NS}/cmd_vel_unstamped', 10)
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(
            LaserScan, f'{NS}/scan', self.on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.tick)   # 10 Hz control
        self.front = self.left = self.right = float('inf')
        self.have_scan = False
        self.n = 0
        self.get_logger().info('wall_follower up; waiting for scan...')

    def sector_min(self, msg, center):
        """Min valid range in a sector centered at angle `center` (rad)."""
        best = float('inf')
        for i, r in enumerate(msg.ranges):
            if not math.isfinite(r) or r <= msg.range_min:
                continue
            a = msg.angle_min + i * msg.angle_increment
            # wrap difference into [-pi, pi]
            d = math.atan2(math.sin(a - center), math.cos(a - center))
            if abs(d) <= SECTOR and r < best:
                best = r
        return best

    def on_scan(self, msg):
        self.front = self.sector_min(msg, 0.0)
        self.left = self.sector_min(msg, math.pi / 2)
        self.right = self.sector_min(msg, -math.pi / 2)
        self.have_scan = True

    def tick(self):
        if not self.have_scan:
            return
        t = Twist()
        if self.front < FRONT_STOP:
            # blocked ahead -> rotate right in place (away from left wall)
            t.linear.x = 0.0
            t.angular.z = -TURN
        elif self.left > TARGET_LEFT + HYST:
            # left opened up (corner/opening) -> curve left to reacquire wall
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED * 0.6
            t.angular.z = TURN * 0.6
        elif self.left < TARGET_LEFT - HYST:
            # too close to left wall -> ease right
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED
            t.angular.z = -TURN * 0.4
        else:
            # good corridor -> straight
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED
            t.angular.z = 0.0
        self.pub.publish(t)
        self.n += 1
        if self.n % 20 == 0:  # ~every 2s
            self.get_logger().info(
                f'front={self.front:.2f} left={self.left:.2f} right={self.right:.2f} '
                f'-> v={t.linear.x:.2f} w={t.angular.z:.2f}')


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = WallFollower()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.pub.publish(Twist())  # stop the robot on exit
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

            d = math.atan2(math.sin(a - center), math.cos(a - center))
            if abs(d) <= SECTOR and r < best:
                best = r
        return best

    def on_scan(self, msg):
        self.front = self.sector_min(msg, 0.0)
        self.left = self.sector_min(msg, math.pi / 2)
        self.right = self.sector_min(msg, -math.pi / 2)
        self.have_scan = True

    def tick(self):
        if not self.have_scan:
            return
        t = Twist()
        if self.front < FRONT_STOP:
            # blocked ahead -> rotate right in place (away from left wall)
            t.linear.x = 0.0
            t.angular.z = -TURN
        elif self.left > TARGET_LEFT + HYST:
            # left opened up (corner/opening) -> curve left to reacquire wall
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED * 0.6
            t.angular.z = TURN * 0.6
        elif self.left < TARGET_LEFT - HYST:
            # too close to left wall -> ease right
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED
            t.angular.z = -TURN * 0.4
        else:
            # good corridor -> straight
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED
            t.angular.z = 0.0
        self.pub.publish(t)
        self.n += 1
        if self.n % 20 == 0:  # ~every 2s
            self.get_logger().info(
                f'front={self.front:.2f} left={self.left:.2f} right={self.right:.2f} '
                f'-> v={t.linear.x:.2f} w={t.angular.z:.2f}')


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = WallFollower()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.pub.publish(Twist())  # stop the robot on exit
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

content.text:
Found the real blocker — and it's not the code. **All 640 lidar beams read exactly `range_min` (0.164 m).** Not varying, not `inf` — every single beam pinned to the sensor's minimum. That's the classic signature of a **broken GPU depth render**: the lidar isn't seeing the world at all, it's returning the near-plane default.

And here's the critical connection — the variable that changed since the lidar last worked (step 1 confirmed valid scans) is exactly **software → d3d12 GPU rendering**. The GPU fix that bought us 4.6× speed may have **broken the GPU-rendered sensors** (offscreen depth rendering via d3d12 on WSL is a known-fragile path — the GUI renders fine while sensor render-targets come back empty).

Let me stop the now-useless wall-follower (it's driving blind) and verify this hypothesis directly:

Camera probe timed out (inconclusive — at RTF 0.07 the preview image may just publish too slowly to catch). Let me stop chasing cheap proxies and run the **decisive** test: the one variable that changed is software→d3d12 rendering, so I'll check the lidar under software (known-good in step 1).

But I'll set up the relaunch to test *multiple* render backends in one go, because there's a promising alternative: **`zink`** (Mesa's OpenGL-on-Vulkan) is also installed, and it often handles offscreen sensor rendering correctly where `d3d12` fails — potentially giving us working sensors *and* GPU speed. Let me make the launcher mode-switchable:

input.old_string:

# GPU rendering via WSLg: Mesa's d3d12 driver on the discrete RTX 3050.
# (LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 was a step-1 crutch that pinned RTF to ~0.015 on llvmpipe.)
# Fallback: unset MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME to use the AMD iGPU; re-add
# LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 (and drop the two lines below) for pure software rendering.
unset LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE
export GALLIUM_DRIVER=d3d12
export MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME=NVIDIA

#   d3d12    = fast (RTF ~0.07) BUT breaks GPU-rendered sensors (lidar all range_min) on WSL.
#   zink     = OpenGL-on-Vulkan; candidate for GPU speed WITH working offscreen sensors.
#   software = llvmpipe; slow (RTF ~0.015) but sensors known-good (step 1).
RENDER="${RENDER:-gpu}"
unset LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE GALLIUM_DRIVER MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME
case "$RENDER" in
  software) export LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 ;;
  zink)     export GALLIUM_DRIVER=zink; export __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=mesa ;;
  gpu|d3d12) export GALLIUM_DRIVER=d3d12; export MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME=NVIDIA ;;
esac
echo "[sim_start] RENDER=$RENDER"

content.text:
That log is decisive — and it reframes the whole problem. Two key things in it:

1. **zink is dead on arrival**: `glx: failed to create drisw screen` → `[GUI] Failed to create OpenGL context` (Qt aborted with a stack trace) → `[OgreRenderEngine] Unable to create glx context` → `X_GLXCreateNewContext BadValue` → Gazebo exited. zink can't create a GL context for Gazebo's OGRE renderer at all.

2. **The real constraint is now clear.** Look at the sensor path: `Sensors.cc: Initializing render context → Loading plugin [gz-rendering-ogre]`. Gazebo renders **sensors through OGRE's GLX path**, same as the GUI. So on this WSL box:

| Backend | Gazebo renders? | Lidar valid? | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| d3d12 | yes | **NO** (all range_min) | fast (0.07) |
| zink | **NO** (GL context fails) | — | — |
| software (llvmpipe) | yes | yes (step 1) | slow (0.015) |

The GPU GL paths either **break offscreen sensor rendering** (d3d12) or **can't init GL at all** (zink). Only **software rendering produces valid sensor data.** That's the environmental truth, and I'm not going to rabbit-hole trying to force d3d12's depth readback to work — that's exactly the mono-directional drilling to avoid.

## This flips the speed strategy

Since we're forced onto **software (CPU) rendering**, the way to reclaim speed is different: in software mode each sensor is a **CPU raytrace**, so **fewer sensors = faster sim**. The "strip sensors" lever you deferred is now the *right and necessary* one — not for GPU latency, but because lidar-only + headless means the CPU raytraces **1 sensor instead of ~10**, plus no GUI render. That could lift software RTF well above 0.015 while keeping a working lidar.

**Revised plan:** software rendering + lean (lidar-only) + headless.

First I need to confirm the linchpin — that software lidar is actually valid this session. Ctrl-C the (now-dead) launch to clean up stragglers, then:

```
RENDER=software bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh
```

Tell me when it's up (~30s) and I'll immediately check the lidar ranges. If they're valid (varying distances, not all 0.164), we build the lean software launch and finally map.

---
name: guidemate-sim-gpu-rendering-fix
description: GuideMate WSL render dilemma — GPU (d3d12) is fast but BREAKS sensors (lidar all range_min); software renders sensors correctly but slow. Must use software + strip sensors for speed.
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: eaf3798d-dd5e-460b-98ce-6a9551e35967
---

**HEADLINE (2026-07-05): On this WSL box, GPU GL rendering BREAKS Gazebo sensors. Use SOFTWARE rendering (`LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1`) for anything that needs lidar/camera.** Do NOT re-try d3d12/zink for the sim — both were fully tested and rejected. `sim_start.sh` supports `RENDER=software|gpu|zink` (default gpu is FAST but SENSOR-BROKEN; use `RENDER=software`).

The render backends, tested (world=maze):
- **d3d12 GPU** (RTX 3050 or AMD iGPU via WSLg): sim runs fast (RTF ~0.067, 4.6x) BUT **all 640 lidar beams read range_min (0.164) = garbage**. GPU renders the GUI fine but offscreen sensor depth readback is broken. Useless for SLAM/nav.
- **zink** (GL-on-Vulkan): Gazebo can't create a GL context at all — `glx: failed to create drisw screen`, OGRE `Unable to create glx context`, Qt aborts, gazebo process dies. Non-viable.
- **software (llvmpipe)**: valid lidar (ranges 1.0-11.6m, 639/640 valid) BUT slow (RTF ~0.015 with GUI + all sensors). THE ONLY MODE WITH WORKING SENSORS.

Why: Gazebo renders sensors through OGRE's GLX path (`Sensors.cc → Loading plugin [gz-rendering-ogre]`), same context type as the GUI. The WSL GPU GL drivers mishandle offscreen render-to-texture depth.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# GuideMate TB4 sim launcher — HEADLESS (no Gazebo GUI) for faster RTF.
# Run in a DEDICATED terminal:  bash ~/robotics/sim_start_headless.sh [world]
set -u
WORLD="${1:-maze}"

# ROS setup.bash isn't `set -u`-clean (references AMENT_TRACE_SETUP_FILES etc.)
set +u
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
set -u
unset ROS_DISCOVERY_SERVER ROS_SUPER_CLIENT FASTRTPS_DEFAULT_PROFILES_FILE \
      ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE FASTDDS_BUILTIN_TRANSPORTS
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0
# GPU rendering via WSLg d3d12 on the RTX 3050 (needed even headless: sensors render on GPU).
unset LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE
export GALLIUM_DRIVER=d3d12
# Adapter is overridable for latency testing: `MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME=AMD bash ...`
# NVIDIA = discrete RTX 3050 (more compute, higher WSL submit latency);
# AMD = on-die iGPU (less compute, lower latency — may win the latency-bound sensor flood).
# AMD iGPU measured marginally best (RTF ~0.069 vs 0.052 on NVIDIA) and frees the 3050.
export MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME="${MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME:-AMD}"

pkill -9 -f "turtlebot4_gz_bringup" 2>/dev/null
pkill -9 -f "ros_gz_bridge"          2>/dev/null
pkill -9 -f "gz sim"                 2>/dev/null
sleep 2
rm -f /dev/shm/fastrtps_* /dev/shm/sem.fastrtps_* /dev/shm/*fastdds* 2>/dev/null

echo "[sim_start_headless] launching HEADLESS TB4 (world=$WORLD, namespace=robot_1) ..."
exec ros2 launch ~/robotics/sim_headless.launch.py \
  namespace:=robot_1 rviz:=false world:="$WORLD"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""GuideMate SLAM driver: reactive left-hand wall-follower (lidar-only).

Drives the namespaced TB4 around a maze to build a slam_toolbox map, hands-off.
- Subscribes /robot_1/scan (SensorDataQoS = BEST_EFFORT, matches the gz lidar).
- Publishes geometry_msgs/Twist to /robot_1/cmd_vel_unstamped (no stamp check).
Left-hand rule: keep the wall on the LEFT at ~target distance; turn right when the
front is blocked; curve left to reacquire when the left opens up. Speeds kept modest
so SLAM scan-matching stays clean (fast rotation smears loop closure).
"""
import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist

NS = '/robot_1'

# tunables
TARGET_LEFT = 0.55     # desired distance to left wall (m)
FRONT_STOP = 0.65      # if anything closer than this ahead, turn away
LIN_SPEED = 0.22       # forward speed (m/s); TB4 max ~0.31
TURN = 0.9             # base angular speed (rad/s)
HYST = 0.12            # deadband around TARGET_LEFT (m)
SECTOR = math.radians(25)  # half-width of each sampling sector


class WallFollower(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('wall_follower')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, f'{NS}/cmd_vel_unstamped', 10)
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(
            LaserScan, f'{NS}/scan', self.on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.tick)   # 10 Hz control
        self.front = self.left = self.right = float('inf')
        self.have_scan = False
        self.n = 0
        self.get_logger().info('wall_follower up; waiting for scan...')

    def sector_min(self, msg, center):
        """Min valid range in a sector centered at angle `center` (rad)."""
        best = float('inf')
        for i, r in enumerate(msg.ranges):
            if not math.isfinite(r) or r <= msg.range_min:
                continue
            a = msg.angle_min + i * msg.angle_increment
            # wrap difference into [-pi, pi]
            d = math.atan2(math.sin(a - center), math.cos(a - center))
            if abs(d) <= SECTOR and r < best:
                best = r
        return best

    def on_scan(self, msg):
        self.front = self.sector_min(msg, 0.0)
        self.left = self.sector_min(msg, math.pi / 2)
        self.right = self.sector_min(msg, -math.pi / 2)
        self.have_scan = True

    def tick(self):
        if not self.have_scan:
            return
        t = Twist()
        if self.front < FRONT_STOP:
            # blocked ahead -> rotate right in place (away from left wall)
            t.linear.x = 0.0
            t.angular.z = -TURN
        elif self.left > TARGET_LEFT + HYST:
            # left opened up (corner/opening) -> curve left to reacquire wall
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED * 0.6
            t.angular.z = TURN * 0.6
        elif self.left < TARGET_LEFT - HYST:
            # too close to left wall -> ease right
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED
            t.angular.z = -TURN * 0.4
        else:
            # good corridor -> straight
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED
            t.angular.z = 0.0
        self.pub.publish(t)
        self.n += 1
        if self.n % 20 == 0:  # ~every 2s
            self.get_logger().info(
                f'front={self.front:.2f} left={self.left:.2f} right={self.right:.2f} '
                f'-> v={t.linear.x:.2f} w={t.angular.z:.2f}')


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = WallFollower()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.pub.publish(Twist())  # stop the robot on exit
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

# tunables

WALL_DETECT = 1.5      # left reading below this => a wall is present to follow
FRONT_STOP = 0.7       # if anything closer than this ahead, turn away
LIN_SPEED = 0.30       # forward speed (m/s); TB4 max ~0.31 (speed = key lever at low RTF)
TURN = 0.8             # base angular speed (rad/s)
HYST = 0.15            # deadband around TARGET_LEFT (m)
SECTOR = math.radians(25)  # half-width of each sampling sector


class WallFollower(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('wall_follower')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, f'{NS}/cmd_vel_unstamped', 10)
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(
            LaserScan, f'{NS}/scan', self.on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.tick)   # 10 Hz control
        self.front = self.left = self.right = float('inf')
        self.have_scan = False
        self.n = 0
        self.get_logger().info('wall_follower up; waiting for scan...')

    def sector_min(self, msg, center):
        """Min valid range in a sector centered at angle `center` (rad)."""
        best = float('inf')
        for i, r in enumerate(msg.ranges):
            if not math.isfinite(r) or r <= msg.range_min:
                continue
            a = msg.angle_min + i * msg.angle_increment
            # wrap difference into [-pi, pi]
            d = math.atan2(math.sin(a - center), math.cos(a - center))
            if abs(d) <= SECTOR and r < best:
                best = r
        return best

    def on_scan(self, msg):
        self.front = self.sector_min(msg, 0.0)
        self.left = self.sector_min(msg, math.pi / 2)
        self.right = self.sector_min(msg, -math.pi / 2)
        self.have_scan = True

    def tick(self):
        if not self.have_scan:
            return
        t = Twist()
        if self.front < FRONT_STOP:
            # blocked ahead -> rotate right in place (away from left wall)
            t.linear.x = 0.0
            t.angular.z = -TURN
        elif self.left > TARGET_LEFT + HYST:
            # left opened up (corner/opening) -> curve left to reacquire wall
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED * 0.6
            t.angular.z = TURN * 0.6
        elif self.left < TARGET_LEFT - HYST:
            # too close to left wall -> ease right
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED
            t.angular.z = -TURN * 0.4
        else:
            # good corridor -> straight
            t.linear.x = LIN_SPEED
            t.angular.z = 0.0
        self.pub.publish(t)
        self.n += 1
        if self.n % 20 == 0:  # ~every 2s
            self.get_logger().info(
                f'front={self.front:.2f} left={self.left:.2f} right={self.right:.2f} '
                f'-> v={t.linear.x:.2f} w={t.angular.z:.2f}')


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = WallFollower()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.pub.publish(Twist())  # stop the robot on exit
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

lines: # blocked ahead -> rotate right in place (away from left wall)
+            # NO left wall nearby (open space) -> drive forward to FIND one,
+            # only a gentle left bias so we spiral out instead of circling in place.
-            # left opened up (corner/opening) -> curve left to reacquire wall
+            # wall present but drifting away -> curve left to close the gap
# too close to left wall -> ease right
+            # good corridor, wall at target distance -> straight

<xacro:macro name="cliff_sensor" params="name gazebo namespace parent:=base_link
                                         visualize:=false *origin">
  <!-- Sensor settings -->
  <xacro:property name="update_rate"         value="62"/>
  <xacro:property name="fov_deg"             value="5"/>
  <xacro:property name="fov_rad"             value="${fov_deg*deg2rad}"/>

  <xacro:property name="max_range"           value="${15*cm2m}"/>
  <xacro:property name="samples"             value="${fov_deg/5}"/>
  <xacro:property name="sensor_name"         value="cliff_${name}"/>
  <xacro:property name="detection_threshold" value="${8*cm2m}"/>


  <joint name="${sensor_name}_joint" type="fixed">
    <xacro:insert_block name="origin"/>
    <parent link="${parent}"/>
    <child link="${sensor_name}"/>
  </joint>

  <link name="${sensor_name}">
    <xacro:inertial_dummy/>
  </link>

  <gazebo reference="${sensor_name}">
    <xacro:ray_sensor sensor_name="${sensor_name}" gazebo="${gazebo}" 
                      update_rate="${update_rate}" visualize="${visualize}" 
                      h_samples="${samples}" h_res="1.0" h_min_angle="-${fov_rad/2}" h_max_angle="${fov_rad/2}"

    </xacro:ray_sensor>

</xacro:macro>

---
name: guidemate-sim-gpu-rendering-fix
description: GuideMate WSL render dilemma — GPU (d3d12) is fast but BREAKS sensors (lidar all range_min); software renders sensors correctly but slow. Must use software + strip sensors for speed.
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: eaf3798d-dd5e-460b-98ce-6a9551e35967
---

**HEADLINE (2026-07-05): On this WSL box, GPU GL rendering BREAKS Gazebo sensors. Use SOFTWARE rendering (`LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1`) for anything that needs lidar/camera.** Do NOT re-try d3d12/zink for the sim — both were fully tested and rejected. `sim_start.sh` supports `RENDER=software|gpu|zink` (default gpu is FAST but SENSOR-BROKEN; use `RENDER=software`).

The render backends, tested (world=maze):
- **d3d12 GPU** (RTX 3050 or AMD iGPU via WSLg): sim runs fast (RTF ~0.067, 4.6x) BUT **all 640 lidar beams read range_min (0.164) = garbage**. GPU renders the GUI fine but offscreen sensor depth readback is broken. Useless for SLAM/nav.
- **zink** (GL-on-Vulkan): Gazebo can't create a GL context at all — `glx: failed to create drisw screen`, OGRE `Unable to create glx context`, Qt aborts, gazebo process dies. Non-viable.
- **software (llvmpipe)**: valid lidar (ranges 1.0-11.6m, 639/640 valid) BUT slow (RTF ~0.015 with GUI + all sensors). THE ONLY MODE WITH WORKING SENSORS.

Why: Gazebo renders sensors through OGRE's GLX path (`Sensors.cc → Loading plugin [gz-rendering-ogre]`), same context type as the GUI. The WSL GPU GL drivers mishandle offscreen render-to-texture depth.

**Speed strategy under software:** each sensor is a CPU raytrace, so speed is reclaimed by (a) headless (drop the GUI's CPU 3D render) and (b) stripping sensors to lidar-only (CPU renders 1 sensor instead of ~10; camera is the heaviest — a full image raster vs 640-ray lidar). This is why the "strip sensors" lever matters — for CPU cost, not GPU latency. In progress: a lean headless+software launch (`~/robotics/sim_start_headless.sh` + `sim_headless.launch.py`, server-only `gz sim -s`).

Also fixed this session: `sim_start.sh` had `set -u` which crashed on ROS `setup.bash` (unbound AMENT_TRACE_SETUP_FILES) — wrapped in `set +u`/`set -u`. `mesa-utils` installed (glxinfo). Clock knob useless below RTF 1.0; robot-SPEED is the only useful runtime speed lever. See [[guidemate-sim-facts]], [[guidemate-mvp-plan]], [[debugging-step-back-over-detail-drilling]].

content.text:
Two ways — quickest first.

## Option 1: Open the saved map image (fastest)

I already rendered the map to a PNG. From WSL, open it in the Windows image viewer:

```
explorer.exe $(wslpath -w ~/robotics/maps/maze_wip.png)
```

(or `cd ~/robotics/maps && explorer.exe maze_wip.png`)

Black = walls, white = driven/free space, gray = unmapped. That's the same image I've been showing you.

## Option 2: RViz — live, interactive view (the proper ROS way)

Shows the map, the robot, and the live laser scan together, updating as SLAM runs:

```
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0 rviz2
```

Then in RViz: set **Fixed Frame** = `map`, click **Add → By topic → `/robot_1/map` → Map**. (Add `/robot_1/scan → LaserScan` too if you want to see the lidar.) It renders via software GL — works, just a bit slow.

## The catch for comparing to the maze shape

content.text:
Four solid questions. Let me take them in order.

## 1. Drawing a complete map by hand (manual teleop)

Yes — manual driving is actually the *reliable* way to get full coverage (it beats the wall-follower precisely because you can deliberately visit the disconnected islands). The setup: keep the sim + SLAM running, drive with the keyboard, watch the map fill in, save when done.

**Drive command** (remap the keyboard teleop onto the topic our robot listens to):
```
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0 ros2 run teleop_twist_keyboard teleop_twist_keyboard \
  --ros-args -r /cmd_vel:=/robot_1/cmd_vel_unstamped
```
(`i/j/k/l` to drive, `q/z` adjust speed. It publishes plain `Twist`, which is exactly what `/robot_1/cmd_vel_unstamped` wants.)

**See where to go while driving** — run RViz alongside it:
```
ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0 rviz2
```
→ Fixed Frame = `map`, Add `/robot_1/map` (Map) + `/robot_1/scan` (LaserScan) + the robot. As you drive into a gray area, you watch it turn into walls/free space. Drive every corridor and around every island until no gray remains inside the maze.

**Save when complete:**
```
ros2 run nav2_map_server map_saver_cli -t /robot_1/map -f ~/robotics/maps/maze --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true
```

One practical note: since we're headless you're navigating by RViz, not by seeing the Gazebo world. If you'd rather see the actual maze while driving, relaunch with the GUI (`bash ~/robotics/sim_start.sh` — it now inherits our physics+sensor speedups, so it's far faster than the original) and drive watching Gazebo + RViz together.

## 2. Why the GPU *destroyed* the lidar (speed ≠ correctness)

This is the key intuition: **faster rendering doesn't mean correct rendering.** The GPU was rendering fine — it was rendering *wrong*.

How a simulated lidar actually works: Gazebo's `gpu_lidar` doesn't do geometry math — it **renders the scene into an offscreen depth buffer** (like a depth-camera) from the sensor's viewpoint, then **reads those depth values back** from GPU memory and converts each to a range. Two GPU operations are involved:
1. Render scene → offscreen render-target texture.
2. **Read the depth texture back to CPU.**

On WSL, there's no native Linux GPU driver — OpenGL calls are **translated to Direct3D 12** (Mesa's `d3d12` driver → Windows GPU). That translation layer is *incomplete*: the **offscreen depth render-to-texture readback path is broken**. The depth buffer comes back empty/near-plane, so every ray reads ~0 → Gazebo clamps to `range_min` (0.164) → all 640 beams identical garbage.

Why did the *GUI* look fine on GPU? On-screen **color** rendering is a well-supported translation path; offscreen **depth readback** (what sensors need) is not. So the window drew a nice maze while the sensor got zeros.

And why does CPU (`llvmpipe`) work? It's slow but implements the full OpenGL spec **correctly**, including depth readback. It's the classic *fast-but-buggy translator vs. slow-but-accurate translator* trade-off. On **native** Linux with a real NVIDIA driver, `gpu_lidar` is both fast *and* correct — it's specifically the WSL d3d12 emulation that's the problem.

## 3. The "message too old / exceeded timeout" warnings — essential to fix?

There are **two severities of the same timestamp mechanism**, and you're seeing the mild one now:

- **The catastrophic case** (what froze SLAM): sim time jumped *backwards* by hundreds of seconds on a sim relaunch. Every message looked ancient → SLAM rejected *all* of them → total freeze. That one **must** be fixed (restart the `use_sim_time` node), and we did.
- **The warnings you're seeing now** ("older than current time by 0.5 s, exceeds timeout"): a scan arrives, but the **TF transform** needed to place it (odom→base→laser at that exact timestamp) isn't in the buffer within the tolerance window, so *that one scan* is dropped. This is normal timing jitter — publishers slightly out of sync, made worse by variable RTF.

**Is it essential? No — as long as the map builds** (and ours did). It just means *some* scans are discarded, so mapping is a bit less dense/efficient. It becomes worth fixing only if the map is too sparse or building too slowly. The fixes, if needed:
- Raise SLAM's `transform_timeout` / `tf_buffer_duration` (give TF more slack).
- Make sure **every** node has `use_sim_time:=true` (a mismatch is the usual culprit).
- Reduce clock jitter.

For now: safe to ignore. It's a symptom of timing slack, not corruption.

## 4. Logic chain of how I "detected"/read the map

I didn't write one monolithic mapping script — I used the standard tool for *saving* and small rclpy probes for *inspecting*. The chain:

**The data model first:** SLAM publishes `/robot_1/map` as a `nav_msgs/OccupancyGrid` — a latched (`TRANSIENT_LOCAL`, `RELIABLE`) message containing:
- `info`: `width`, `height`, `resolution` (0.05 m/cell), `origin` pose.
- `data`: a flat `int8[]`, row-major, one value per cell: **−1 = unknown, 0 = free, 100 = occupied** (0–100 = occupancy probability).

**(a) Saving** — `map_saver_cli` (from `nav2_map_server`): subscribes to that OccupancyGrid, thresholds it (free < 0.25, occupied > 0.65), and writes two files: `maze_wip.pgm` (a grayscale image: black=wall, white=free, gray=unknown) + `maze_wip.yaml` (resolution, origin, thresholds — what Nav2 later loads).

**(b) Coverage inspection** — my little rclpy snippet:
1. Subscribe to `/robot_1/map` with `TRANSIENT_LOCAL`+`RELIABLE` QoS (must match the latched publisher, or you get nothing — same QoS lesson from step 1).
2. Spin until one message arrives.
3. Walk `data`: count `v<0` (unknown), `0≤v<50` (free), `v≥50` (occupied).
4. Coverage = known/total; open area = free_cells × resolution² m².

**(c) Visual check** — PIL: `Image.open('maze_wip.pgm').resize(2×, NEAREST).save('.png')`, then I read the PNG to actually *look* at the shape (map_saver's .pgm isn't directly viewable in my image reader; PNG is).

**(d) The scan-validity probe** (how I caught the range_min garbage) — subscribe `/robot_1/scan` (`LaserScan`) with `SensorDataQoS` (BEST_EFFORT), then count beams that are `finite AND > range_min`. All-invalid → broken sensor.

**(e) RTF** — `gz topic -e -t /world/maze/stats`, pull the `real_time_factor` field, average a few samples.

So the "detection" is really: **OccupancyGrid → threshold/count (coverage) or PGM→PNG (visual); LaserScan → validity count; gz stats → RTF.** Each is a tiny targeted probe rather than one big script.

content.text:
Now I see exactly what you're getting at — and yes, on both counts. You've hit on something important for a guidance robot.

## The map is a plain, editable raster — hand-authoring is standard practice

A Nav2 map is **not** a special SLAM artifact. It's literally:
- a **`.pgm` grayscale image** — one pixel per grid cell, and
- a **`.yaml`** giving `resolution` (metres per pixel), `origin`, and the thresholds.

The occupancy convention in the image:

| Pixel | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **black (≈0)** | occupied — **wall** |
| **white (≈254)** | free — open space |
| **mid-gray (205)** | unknown |

And the YAML that binds it:
```yaml
image: maze.pgm
resolution: 0.05          # metres per pixel
origin: [-x, -y, 0.0]     # world coords of the pixel at the bottom-left
occupied_thresh: 0.65     # darker than this ⇒ wall
free_thresh: 0.25         # lighter than this ⇒ free
negate: 0
```

So you can open the `.pgm` in **GIMP / Krita / even Paint**, **draw a black line = "this is a wall," leave white = open space, gray = unknown**, save, and Nav2's `map_server` loads it *identically* to a SLAM-made map. There's nothing sacred about how the pixels got there.

## Your glass-door instinct is exactly right — and this is *why* hand-editing matters

A SLAM map only records **what the laser physically returns**. So lidar is blind or wrong to:
- **glass doors / windows** → laser passes through → mapped as open (robot drives into it),
- **mirrors** → false reflections → phantom walls,
- **thin poles / chair legs / table edges** → too small to hit reliably,
- **down-stairs / ledges** → a 2D lidar can't see a drop at all.

The standard fix is precisely what you described: **SLAM a rough map, then hand-annotate it** — paint the glass door as a solid black wall, block off the stairwell, thicken thin obstacles. For GuideMate this isn't cosmetic, it's *safety*: you're encoding hazards the sensor can't perceive. So the real workflow is **auto-SLAM → manual correction**, not either/or.

## Your sub-question: yes, I can render *data → image* reversibly (author a map from scratch)

Everything I did was image-*reading*. The reverse is straightforward — I write a small authoring script where **you specify geometry in metres** and it rasterizes to the exact occupancy convention:

- You give it: a **resolution** (say 0.05 m — see note below), the map extent, and a list of **walls as line segments or rectangles in world metres** (plus optionally "this region is free," "this is unknown").
- It paints: **black (0) along the wall lines**, **white (254) for declared free space**, **gray (205) for unknown**, and writes matching `.pgm` + `.yaml`.
- Same tool can **edit an existing SLAM map** — e.g., load `maze.pgm`, draw a black line where the glass door is, re-save.

To keep it rigorous: pure **black (0)** and pure **white (254/255)** are unambiguous under any threshold — those are the safe values to paint. I'd also have the script **round-trip verify** (load it back as an OccupancyGrid and confirm each region reads as wall/free/unknown as intended), so we *prove* the reverse mapping is correct rather than assume it.

**On resolution (your "0.5 m" example):** resolution is just the YAML number, so you *can* use 0.5 m/cell — but that's coarse. A TB4 is ~0.35 m wide, so at 0.5 m each pixel is bigger than the robot: walls become blocky and the planner loses tight gaps. **0.05 m (5 cm)** is the standard for indoor nav — precise enough for doorways. Use coarse only if you want a deliberately smaller/faster map. The choice is one line in the YAML; the authoring script would take it as a parameter.

---

So you have three composable paths now:
1. **Auto** — SLAM (fast but misses islands/glass),
2. **Manual drive** — teleop + RViz to fill coverage,
3. **Hand-authored/edited map** — draw walls directly, and correct SLAM's blind spots (glass doors, stairs).

Want me to build that map-authoring/editing script — parameterized by resolution, taking wall segments in metres, with the round-trip verification — so you can either author the maze layout directly or patch the SLAM map's gaps and glass-door-type hazards?

## Q2 first, because it changes the whole game: yes, Gazebo hands you exact geometry

The `maze.sdf` **is** ground truth. Every wall has a `<pose>` (position + orientation, in metres) and a `<box><size>` (length × width × height, in metres). So the length of *any* wall is sitting right there — wall1 of the border is exactly 20 m long, 1 cm thick, centred at x = −10.005. No driving, no measuring, no sensor error.

Runtime, you can also get it live if you prefer: `gz model -m <name> --pose`, the `/world/maze/scene/info` topic, or in the Gazebo GUI just click a wall → its size shows in the inspector. But the SDF file is the cleanest source.

**The punchline:** since we *have* the true world, the fastest path to a **complete, exact** map isn't SLAM or hand-drawing at all — it's to **parse the SDF and rasterize every wall-box straight into an occupancy grid** at whatever resolution you pick. That gives a perfect, fully-covered map (including the islands the wall-follower couldn't reach) in one pass, in seconds. This is "ground-truth map generation," and for a sim it's the standard shortcut.

## Q1: your calibration idea — right instinct, but aimed at the wrong case

Here's the correction: a **SLAM map is already metric.** The resolution isn't something you *discover* by driving a known wall — it's a number *you set* (0.05 m/pixel). SLAM fuses odometry + scan, both in metres, so 1 pixel = resolution metres *by construction*. There's no hidden scale factor to calibrate out.

**Where your instinct is exactly correct:** when you're **tracing an unknown-scale image** — an architect's floor plan photo, a screenshot, a CAD export with no units. Then you *do* need one known reference length: measure a wall you know is 5 m, see it spans 100 pixels → set `resolution = 0.05`. That's real, and it's the standard blueprint-tracing calibration. So the technique belongs to "trace a picture," not "SLAM output."

And the broader workflow you described — *drive a little to get a correctly-scaled, correctly-oriented anchor, then draw the rest by hand* — is a legitimate time-saver. The value isn't scale discovery; it's getting a real, aligned frame to trace over.

## How people actually save time on maps (the menu)

| Situation | Fast path |
|---|---|
| **You have the sim world** (us!) | Generate the map **directly from the SDF geometry** — exact, complete, seconds |
| Have a CAD / floor-plan image | Trace it; calibrate scale with one known dimension (**your idea**) |
| Real building, no plan | SLAM once, then **hand-patch** blind spots (glass, stairs, thin obstacles) |
| Any of the above | Coarser resolution for speed, reuse/stitch partial maps |

One honest caveat on the SDF-derived map: it's *ground truth*, not "what the robot's lidar perceives." Usually that's a feature (perfect + complete). It only bites you if you specifically want to test how well the robot *localizes* against an imperfect map — but our maze has no glass/mirrors, so the ground-truth map ≈ what the lidar sees anyway. For MVP #1 it's ideal.

The file makes this **very** clean — here's what I found and what it means:

- **3 models:** `ground_plane` (ignore), `border` (4 outer walls), `obstacles` (~37 interior walls). 42 links total.
- **No rotated walls** — every pose has yaw 0. That's the big simplifier: every wall is an **axis-aligned box**, so rasterization is trivial (no rotated-rectangle math).
- **Sizes** confirm it: thin partition walls (`0.01 × 20 × 2`, `20 × 0.01 × 2`) and blocky obstacles (`1×2`, `2×9`, etc.), heights 1–2 m — all far above the 0.19 m lidar, so all are real obstacles. The `100×100` is just the floor.
- Maze spans ~20×20 m centred on the origin.

## Can I retrieve the world and generate a map directly? Yes — unambiguously.

Two possible routes:
- **(a) Parse the static `maze.sdf`** — read every `border`/`obstacles` link's pose + box size straight from the file. No sim, no GPU, no RTF, deterministic.
- (b) Query the running sim at runtime (`gz model`, scene-info topic).

**Route (a) wins decisively** — it's ground truth, sim-independent (so the ~0.02 RTF is irrelevant), and repeatable. That's what I'll use.

## The plan

1. **Parse** `border` + `obstacles` models → list of axis-aligned wall rectangles in **world metres** (center x,y ± size/2). Skip `ground_plane` and lights.
2. **Frame + bounds:** compute map extent from wall min/max (+ small margin), pick resolution, and — critically — set the YAML `origin` so the **map frame = Gazebo world frame** (pixel (0,0) ↔ known world coords).
3. **Rasterize:** fill interior = free (white); stamp each wall rectangle as occupied (black); mark outside-the-border = unknown (gray).
4. **Write** `.pgm` + `.yaml` (world-frame origin, resolution, standard thresholds).
5. **Verify** three ways: round-trip load as an OccupancyGrid, render a PNG to eyeball, and **overlay against our partial SLAM map + the robot's spawn point (world 0,0)** to prove both the geometry *and* the frame alignment are right.

## Three technical risks I'm watching (and how I handle them)

- **Frame alignment (the crucial one):** the map must be in the **Gazebo world frame**, because later we'll capture destination poses from `/robot_1/sim_ground_truth_pose` (world frame) and Nav2 must agree. I verify by checking that world (0,0) lands in free space and that walls line up with the SLAM map.
- **Thin-wall disappearance:** a 0.01 m wall is thinner than a 0.05 m pixel — a naive "is the cell *center* inside the wall?" test would make walls vanish. I use a **cell-rectangle *intersection*** test so every thin wall becomes a continuous 1-pixel line.
- **Map vs. costmap inflation:** I keep the static map as **true geometry** (no inflation) — Nav2's costmap inflates walls at runtime. Baking inflation in would double it.

## Two choices I want your call on before I write it

1. **Resolution:** I recommend **0.05 m** (5 cm — standard indoor nav). Coarser (e.g. 0.5 m) would be blocky and lose gaps. OK with 0.05?
2. **Outside-the-border cells:** I recommend **unknown (gray)** so the robot treats the world as bounded by the border. Alternative is "free" — but unknown is safer/cleaner. OK?

If you're good with 0.05 m + unknown-outside, I'll write the SDF→map generator (reusable for your future DIY worlds too) and run the three-way verification. Anything you'd change?

content.text:
Good instinct, and let me sharpen it because the distinction matters:

The `.pgm` is a **2D grid of values, not a list of positions.** Two parts do two jobs:
- **Where** a cell is comes from its **index** in the array — row `r`, column `c` → world position `(x,y) = (origin_x + c·res, origin_y + (rows−r)·res)`. The coordinate is *implicit* in the index; it's not stored.
- **What's there** is the **number stored** at that index: `0`=wall (black), `254`=free (white), `205`=unknown (gray).

So it's a dense raster (like a photo — every cell has a value), **not** a vector list of `(x, y, wall?)` tuples. The `resolution` + `origin` in the YAML are what turn "index" into "metres." That's the whole trick.

Good — 0.05 m, unknown-outside, going ahead. Let me write the generator:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate a Nav2 occupancy-grid map directly from a Gazebo world SDF.

Ground-truth map generation: parse every axis-aligned wall box (pose + size) from
the world's static models, rasterize their footprints into a .pgm + .yaml at a
chosen resolution, in the GAZEBO WORLD FRAME (so it aligns with the robot's pose
and future destination coordinates). No sim, no SLAM, no GPU — pure file parsing.

Convention (Nav2 map_server): pixel 0=occupied(black), 254=free(white), 205=unknown.
Free = cells reachable from the robot spawn by flood-fill; everything else = unknown.

Usage: python3 sdf_to_map.py <world.sdf> <out_basename> [resolution] [spawn_x] [spawn_y]
"""
import sys, math, collections
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

SDF        = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else \
             '/opt/ros/jazzy/share/irobot_create_gz_bringup/worlds/maze.sdf'
OUT        = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else '/home/baishibo123/robotics/maps/maze_truth'
RES        = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 0.05
SPAWN      = (float(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 0.0,
             float(sys.argv[5]) if len(sys.argv) > 5 else 0.0)
MARGIN     = 0.5                       # m of border around the extent
WALL_MODELS = {'border', 'obstacles'}  # models to treat as obstacles (skip ground_plane/lights)
OCC, FREE, UNK = 0, 254, 205

def pose_xy(elem):
    """x,y from an element's first <pose> child (or 0,0)."""
    p = elem.find('pose')
    if p is None or not p.text:
        return 0.0, 0.0
    v = p.text.split()
    return float(v[0]), float(v[1])

def parse_walls(sdf):
    """Return list of (x0,x1,y0,y1) world-frame footprints for wall boxes."""
    root = ET.parse(sdf).getroot()
    world = root.find('world')
    rects, border_rects = [], []
    for model in world.findall('model'):
        name = model.get('name')
        if name not in WALL_MODELS:
            continue
        mx, my = pose_xy(model)
        for link in model.findall('link'):
            lx, ly = pose_xy(link)
            cx, cy = mx + lx, my + ly
            # first box geometry (prefer collision, else visual)
            box = None
            for tag in ('collision', 'visual'):
                for c in link.findall(tag):
                    b = c.find('geometry/box/size')
                    if b is not None and b.text:
                        box = b.text.split(); break
                if box: break
            if not box or len(box) < 2:
                continue
            sx, sy = float(box[0]), float(box[1])
            r = (cx - sx/2, cx + sx/2, cy - sy/2, cy + sy/2)
            rects.append(r)
            if name == 'border':
                border_rects.append(r)
    return rects, border_rects

def main():
    rects, border = parse_walls(SDF)
    if not rects:
        print('NO WALLS PARSED'); return
    # map extent from all walls + margin (world frame)
    min_x = min(r[0] for r in rects) - MARGIN
    max_x = max(r[1] for r in rects) + MARGIN
    min_y = min(r[2] for r in rects) - MARGIN
    max_y = max(r[3] for r in rects) + MARGIN
    W = int(math.ceil((max_x - min_x) / RES))
    H = int(math.ceil((max_y - min_y) / RES))
    grid = np.full((H, W), UNK, dtype=np.uint8)

    def cell(x, y):
        c = int((x - min_x) / RES)
        r = int((max_y - y) / RES)          # row 0 = top = max_y
        return r, c

    # stamp walls occupied (intersection test: any cell the rect touches, so 1cm walls survive)
    occ_mask = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=bool)
    for x0, x1, y0, y1 in rects:
        c0 = max(0, int((x0 - min_x) / RES)); c1 = min(W-1, int((x1 - min_x) / RES))
        r0 = max(0, int((max_y - y1) / RES)); r1 = min(H-1, int((max_y - y0) / RES))
        occ_mask[r0:r1+1, c0:c1+1] = True

    # flood-fill FREE from the spawn cell through non-wall cells
    sr, sc = cell(*SPAWN)
    free_mask = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=bool)
    if 0 <= sr < H and 0 <= sc < W and not occ_mask[sr, sc]:
        dq = collections.deque([(sr, sc)]); free_mask[sr, sc] = True
        while dq:
            r, c = dq.popleft()
            for dr, dc in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)):
                nr, nc = r+dr, c+dc
                if 0 <= nr < H and 0 <= nc < W and not free_mask[nr,nc] and not occ_mask[nr,nc]:
                    free_mask[nr,nc] = True; dq.append((nr,nc))
    else:
        print(f'WARNING: spawn cell ({sr},{sc}) invalid/occupied; free region empty')

    grid[free_mask] = FREE
    grid[occ_mask]  = OCC   # walls last, on top of free

    # write pgm + yaml
    Image.fromarray(grid, 'L').save(OUT + '.pgm')
    with open(OUT + '.yaml', 'w') as f:
        f.write(f"image: {OUT.split('/')[-1]}.pgm\nmode: trinary\n"
                f"resolution: {RES}\norigin: [{min_x:.4f}, {min_y:.4f}, 0.0]\n"
                f"negate: 0\noccupied_thresh: 0.65\nfree_thresh: 0.25\n")
    # viewable png (2x)
    Image.fromarray(grid, 'L').resize((W*2, H*2), Image.NEAREST).save(OUT + '.png')

    # report + verification stats
    nocc, nfree, nunk = int(occ_mask.sum()), int(free_mask.sum()), int((grid==UNK).sum())
    print(f'walls parsed: {len(rects)} (border={len(border)})')
    print(f'extent world: x[{min_x:.2f},{max_x:.2f}] y[{min_y:.2f},{max_y:.2f}]  grid {W}x{H} @ {RES}m')
    print(f'origin (yaml): [{min_x:.3f}, {min_y:.3f}]   spawn(0,0) cell=({sr},{sc}) free={free_mask[sr,sc] if 0<=sr<H and 0<=sc<W else "OOB"}')
    print(f'cells: occ={nocc} free={nfree} unknown={nunk}  free_area={nfree*RES*RES:.1f} m2')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

3. Check what fraction of endpoints land on truth-map walls. High % = map and world share the same frame → safe for Nav2.

The design choice to discuss:
- **Single pose (quick):** sample once at spawn (0,0). Fast, validates one spot + confirms no gross flip/offset.
- **Multi-pose (thorough):** rotate the robot in place and/or nudge it to 2–3 spots, accumulate all beam endpoints, overlay on the truth map. Catches subtle rotation/scale errors a single symmetric pose might miss, and gives a nice visual overlay.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Validate the ground-truth map against live lidar, in the WORLD frame.

Stationary at spawn: the RPLIDAR is 360deg, so one scan sees all directions.
Collect a few scans, transform every beam endpoint to world coords via the
ground-truth pose, and overlay them (red) on the truth map. Red points should
sit exactly on the black walls. Red sticking PAST a wall => that wall is too
short/missing in the map (Shibo's west-wall question).

Run after: bash ~/robotics/sim_start_headless.sh   (no SLAM needed)
"""
import math, numpy as np, yaml
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan
from nav_msgs.msg import Odometry
from PIL import Image

BASE = '/home/baishibo123/robotics/maps/maze_truth'
y = yaml.safe_load(open(BASE + '.yaml'))
res = y['resolution']; ox, oy = y['origin'][0], y['origin'][1]
gray = np.array(Image.open(BASE + '.pgm').convert('L'))
H, W = gray.shape

rclpy.init(); n = Node('scan_check'); buf = {'scans': []}
def on_scan(m): buf['scans'].append((m, buf.get('pose')))
def on_pose(m): buf['pose'] = m.pose.pose
n.create_subscription(LaserScan, '/robot_1/scan', on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data)
n.create_subscription(Odometry, '/robot_1/sim_ground_truth_pose', on_pose, qos_profile_sensor_data)

# collect ~15 scans
n_wait = 0
while len([s for s in buf['scans'] if s[1] is not None]) < 15 and n_wait < 200:
    rclpy.spin_once(n, timeout_sec=0.1); n_wait += 1

scans = [s for s in buf['scans'] if s[1] is not None]
print(f'collected {len(scans)} scans with pose')
if not scans:
    print('NO scan+pose — is the sim up (software headless)?'); rclpy.shutdown(); exit()

rgb = np.stack([gray, gray, gray], axis=-1)
hit = tot = 0
p0 = scans[-1][1]
print(f'robot world pose x={p0.position.x:.2f} y={p0.position.y:.2f}')
for s, p in scans:
    q = p.orientation
    yaw = math.atan2(2*(q.w*q.z+q.x*q.y), 1-2*(q.y*q.y+q.z*q.z))
    px, py = p.position.x, p.position.y
    for i, r in enumerate(s.ranges):
        if not math.isfinite(r) or r <= s.range_min or r >= s.range_max:
            continue
        a = yaw + s.angle_min + i*s.angle_increment
        wx = px + r*math.cos(a); wy = py + r*math.sin(a)
        c = int((wx-ox)/res); row = int(H-(wy-oy)/res)
        if 0 <= row < H and 0 <= c < W:
            tot += 1
            rgb[row, c] = [255, 0, 0]                    # scan return = red
            if (gray[max(0,row-2):row+3, max(0,c-2):c+3] < 50).any():
                hit += 1
# mark robot pose green
rc = int((p0.position.x-ox)/res); rr = int(H-(p0.position.y-oy)/res)
if 0 <= rr < H and 0 <= rc < W:
    rgb[max(0,rr-2):rr+3, max(0,rc-2):rc+3] = [0, 180, 0]

out = BASE + '_scancheck.png'
Image.fromarray(rgb, 'RGB').resize((W*2, H*2), Image.NEAREST).save(out)
print(f'scan endpoints on a truth wall (+-2 cells): {hit}/{tot} = {100*hit/max(tot,1):.0f}%')
print(f'overlay saved: {out}  (red=scan return, green=robot, black=map wall)')
rclpy.shutdown()
